title: Trump upset 'biggest drop in gasoline in 18 years' came after election - USA Today

 Keith Laing USA TODAY Updated Nov. 19, 2026, 10:18 a.m. ET Hear this story President Donald Trump questioned the timing of a recent drop in gas prices, suggesting it was delayed until after the midterm elections.
 Experts attribute the falling prices to seasonal factors, such as lower demand and the switch to cheaper winter-blend gasoline, not politics.
 Despite the recent decline, gas prices remain higher than a year ago, and November 2026 has been the most expensive on record for gas.
 President Donald Trump complained about the fact that gas prices have fallen significantly since the election, after voters registered their frustration with high prices for fuel and other things.
 "Biggest drop in gasoline in 18 years," Trump said in a Nov. 17 post on his Truth Social platform. "Notice that they waited until after the 'Election?'"
 According to a USA TODAY review of data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration , Trump is correct that the drop in gas prices this month is the biggest one that has happened in nearly two decades. But experts say he is wrong to tie the drop to politics.
 The EIA's data shows the biggest one-month drop in average gas prices since 1990 took place in October 2008, when the average fell $1.08 cents from $3.84 a gallon on October 6, 2008 to $2.40 on the week of November 3, 2008. The average price of gas has fallen 57 cents from October 19 to November 19 this year.
 The average price of gas on Thursday, Nov. 19, was $3.72, according to AAA . That's down from an average of $3.90 one week ago on Nov. 12 and an average of $4.29 one month ago on Oct. 19. But it's up from an average of $3.09 a year ago on Nov. 19, 2025.
 Voters consistently said in polls leading up to the 2026 midterm elections that gas prices were top of mind. Trump went into Election Day with higher gas prices than his recent predecessors . He promised in campaign rallies leading up to the election that the prices would drop soon, even as AAA's average national gas price remained above $4 per gallon for most of the year.
 The national average price of gas rose above $4 per gallon for the first time in April and it stayed there from July to the beginning of November, due in large part to the Iran war Trump launched in late February 2026, according to AAA.
 "Crude oil prices have been falling, and gas stations are selling winter-blend gasoline, which is cheaper to produce," AAA said.
 "Gasoline demand also decreases during autumn, which brings down pump prices. But the current national average is still higher than normal for this time of year," the group continued. "So far, this month is the most expensive November on record for gas prices."

Here's why Want to test a car for days before buying it? Here's one way you can What's new with the 2027 Toyota Tundra, and would I recommend it? Why are gas prices falling after the election?
 Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a Nov. 9 blog post that the decline in prices has little to do with the election results, despite the timing of the drop.
 "Gas prices have fallen in the 30 days leading up to the election every year since 2006 except 2010, and it’s typically seasonal: refiners finish maintenance and ramp up output just as demand fades with cooler weather," he wrote. "Those same forces, along with more oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, are why prices could stay below $4 in the weeks ahead."
 The U.S. Energy Information Administration also said seasonal changes to the composition of gas and demand for fuel as Americans take fewer road trips in colder weather months typically lowers prices at the pump in winter months.
 "Historically, retail gasoline prices tend to gradually rise in the spring and peak in late summer, when people drive more frequently," the agency said.
 "Environmental regulations require that gasoline sold in the summer be less prone to evaporate during warm weather," the EIA added. "This requirement means that refiners must replace cheaper (but more evaporative) gasoline components with less evaporative but more expensive components."
 But De Haan said voters sent a clear message to Washington that they want lower fuel prices. Already, a crop of newly elected Democratic senators are talking about suspending the 18.4-cent-per-gallon federal gas tax to bring immediate relief to drivers at the pump.
 "The election’s outcome may send a message to Washington to sharpen its focus on affordability, and I’d expect even more attention on bringing prices down," De Haan said. "But for now, it’s the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump.”
 Trump and some U.S. lawmakers also floated the idea of suspending the federal gas tax to help drivers feeling the pinch at the pump before the election, making it a potential area of bipartisan agreement starting in January when Democrats take control of Congress.
 How did gas prices affect Trump's approval ratings leading into the election?
 Seventy-six percent of registered U.S. voters disapproved of Trump's handling of gas prices, while only 20% approved, according to an Oct. 8 poll from Navigator Research .
 The poll also showed that 73% of registered voters disapproved of Trump's handling of inflation and the cost of living, while only 23% approved. In the poll, 62% of registered voters said they disapproved of how Trump is handling his job as president, while only 36% approved.
 " President Trump ’s approval ratings have hit all-time lows in Navigator tracking," the group said. "Majorities disapprove of Trump’s handling of gas prices, inflation and the cost of living, and foreign policy."
 On Election Day, Democratic candidates won in every battleground state that political analysts said would likely determine control of the Senate next year and Democrats won at least 254 seats in the House, according to the USA TODAY Election Tracker .
 What are the biggest gas price drop in recent history?
 According to the U.S. EIA , here are the 5 biggest four-week drops on record:
 Oct. 6 to Nov. 3, 2008 : $3.48 to $2.40 ($1.08 difference)
 Sept. 29 to Oct. 27, 2008 : $3.62 to $2.65 (96 cent difference)
 Oct. 13 to Nov. 10, 2008 : $3.15 to $2.22 (92 cent difference)
 Oct. 20 to Nov. 17, 2008 : $2.91 to $2.07 (84 cent difference)
